{"id": "92:5/q15", "question": "What other sura facts are recorded with this verse?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "92:5/q15/p1", "position": "Its titles include al-Layl, wa-al-Layl, and wa-al-Layl idhā yaghshā; a count of twenty verses is given.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr says al-Bukhārī and al-Tirmidhī use the last title and places the sura ninth in revelation order."}]}
{"id": "92:5/q16", "question": "How does the open wording of this passage extend beyond verse 5?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "92:5/q16/p1", "position": "Unspecified objects and nouns keep deeds, belief, and outcomes broad.", "reasons": "Al-Sāmarrāʾī says al-ḥusnā may denote Paradise, good life, good word, future outcome or sound creed, and prefers all these since no noun is supplied, citing 7:180. Likewise yusrā embraces helping others, ease in one's own affairs, and Paradise, with 65:2–4 and 13:18; the contrasting hardship culminates in Hell. He says the sūra leaves oath, answer, actions, agents and outcomes unrestricted. Rāzī reports future wording as certainty (2:21), room for repentance, or deferred afterlife reward; al-Sāmarrāʾī sees the prefixed sīn as assurance, comparing 87:8."}, {"id": "92:5/q16/p2", "position": "The opposing clauses map virtues and vices to different forms of ease and hardship.", "reasons": "Al-Sāmarrāʾī maps giving to easing others, piety to one's circumstances and faith to Paradise; self-sufficiency instead breeds tyranny and hardship for self and others, citing 96:6–7. Al-Burhān treats the opposite traits as a shared condition."}]}
{"id": "92:5/q17", "question": "What non-final vowel treatment is reported in comparable recitation routes?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "92:5/q17/p1", "position": "Some routes open such forms, while others read between vowels where yāʾ is written.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jazarī reports Abū ʿAmr's usual treatment on imāla routes and al-Azraq from Warsh opening in routes through Ibn Ghalbūn, while al-Taysīr and related routes use the intermediate pronunciation; the cited comparison is fa-ammā man ṭaghā."}]}
{"id": "92:5/q18", "question": "How is the passage cited in descriptions of Paradise?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "92:5/q18/p1", "position": "The Prophet cited the promise attached to human work among verses describing Paradise.", "reasons": "Al-Burhān reports that he also cited 32:17 for unseen delights and 56:30 for the tree's long shade."}]}
{"id": "92:5/q19", "question": "What later usage of taqwā-related terms is noted?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "92:5/q19/p1", "position": "The plural muttaqūn emerges later alongside growing mention of disbelievers and believers.", "reasons": "Corpus Coranicum places it in groups IIIa and IIIb and cites 78:31, 77:41, 69:48, 68:34, 52:17 and 51:15."}]}
{"id": "92:5/q20", "question": "How do the giver's deeds relate to later facilitation?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "92:5/q20/p1", "position": "Giving, piety, and belief cause God to enable continued good conduct.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr says the relative clause makes facilitation a reward for those deeds and helps the person persist; describing their deeds as easy praises them, as at 87:8."}]}
{"id": "92:5/q21", "question": "Whom do the opposing three traits characterize?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "92:5/q21/p1", "position": "The combined opposing traits characterize a polytheist.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr contrasts them with the positive traits that mark a believer."}]}
{"id": "92:5/q22", "question": "How does the sura frame wealth and God's ownership?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "92:5/q22/p1", "position": "Givers seek the Hereafter while misers seek the present world, though both lives belong to God.", "reasons": "Al-Sāmarrāʾī says this calls people to God's guidance in both lives. He says the emphatic lām in the ownership statement suits this sura's repeated concern with wealth, unlike the wealth-free context of 53:25."}]}
{"id": "92:5/q23", "question": "How can 'easing toward hardship' be expressed?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "92:5/q23/p1", "position": "It may mirror the phrase for ease rhetorically, or the verb may mean 'prepare' for either outcome.", "reasons": "Al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī offers both ways of understanding the wording."}]}
{"id": "92:6/q01", "question": "What does affirming mean here?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "92:6/q01/p1", "position": "Assenting to the truth of God's promise also entails seeking it and acting accordingly.", "reasons": "Al-Biqāʿī defines taṣdīq as assent that makes the informant's statement true for the believer. {"id": "92:6/q02", "question": "What is the form and lexical sense of al-ḥusnā?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "92:6/q02/p1", "position": "It is the feminine superlative of aḥsan, literally 'the best' or 'most beautiful,' with an understood feminine noun.", "reasons": "Jishumī calls it the supreme blessing for its excellent outcome. Ibn ʿĀshūr allows an omitted noun such as reward, victory, promise or outcome; Islāḥī supplies ʿāqibah, fate or outcome. Bint al-Shāṭiʾ distinguishes material beauty from moral good and cites al-Rāghib's distinction: ḥusn applies to objects and events, ḥasana as a noun to events, and ḥusnā only to events; she notes its opposition to sawʾa."}]}
{"id": "92:6/q03", "question": "What does al-ḥusnā refer to in this verse?", "turns_on": "Whether the feminine superlative designates a creed or truthful word, a promised result, a particular act, divine gifts, or a broad good; some sources explicitly treat several glosses as convergent.", "positions": [{"id": "92:6/q03/p1", "position": "God's promised replacement or compensation for what the giver spends.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī prefers this because the preceding giver seeks recompense and the angel report prays for replacement; al-Qurṭubī reports this preference. Al-Rāzī cites 34:39 and 2:261: replacement exceeds spending, while doubting it is bad opinion of God. Abū Ḥayyān specifies a sworn promise of reward in this world; al-Ālūsī reports worldly return with increase. Ibn ʿAṭiyya points to the angels' prayer."}, {"id": "92:6/q03/p2", "position": "The testimony of God's oneness, 'there is no god but God.'", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī says giving and restraint do not avail without faith in unity and prophecy, citing 90:14–17. Al-Bayḍāwī calls this a true, beautiful statement. Al-Biqāʿī extends the word of justice to monotheism's implications: afterlife promises, replacement in this life, Islam's eventual dominance and the Messenger's promises. Al-Ālūsī prefers tawḥīd together with all required beliefs in a comprehensive account of giving, piety and faith. Study Quran attributes the testimony to most commentators."}, {"id": "92:6/q03/p3", "position": "Paradise, the finest reward.", "reasons": "Mujāhid and others cite 10:26, which promises al-ḥusnā and more to good doers; Study Quran cites 3:148 and 3:195. Ubayy b. Kaʿb reports the Prophet directly answering 'Paradise' when asked, with Ibn Kathīr giving no grading. Al-Rāzī treats reward and Paradise as equivalent here."}, {"id": "92:6/q03/p4", "position": "Reward or recompense in general.", "reasons": "Al-Qurṭubī says the proposed meanings converge on reward, ultimately Paradise; al-Rāzī likewise equates reward with Paradise. Qatāda relates recompense to the giving and piety just mentioned; Khuṣayf gives the general gloss."}, {"id": "92:6/q03/p5", "position": "God's promise to reward the believer, without specifying the reward.", "reasons": "Qatāda says the believer trusts God's promise and acts for it; al-Baghawī notes that God will fulfill it. Al-Bayḍāwī calls it the true, good promise."}, {"id": "92:6/q03/p6", "position": "The beautiful religion of Islam.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī reports this from ʿIkrima and a group, also from Ibn ʿAbbās."}, {"id": "92:6/q03/p7", "position": "Faith or the creed as a whole.", "reasons": "Sayyid Quṭb calls al-ḥusnā an identifying designation of the creed. Kur'an Yolu prefers the whole of Islamic belief and practice, including creed, worship, social dealings and ethics. Study Quran notes a gloss of belief in God. Al-Ālūsī includes all required beliefs in his preferred comprehensive reading."}, {"id": "92:6/q03/p8", "position": "Prayer, almsgiving and fasting.", "reasons": "This gloss is attributed to Zayd b. Aslam; Ibn Kathīr separately transmits from him the end-of-Ramadan charity."}, {"id": "92:6/q03/p9", "position": "The blessings God has bestowed on the person.", "reasons": "Māwardī and Ibn al-Jawzī attribute this to ʿAṭāʾ; Ibn Kathīr reports it from ʿIkrima."}, {"id": "92:6/q03/p10", "position": "The best or good outcome promised for virtuous deeds.", "reasons": "Elmalılı prefers the better reward and final outcome, or the verses promising it, citing 10:26 and 29:7; he also cites 42:23, 53:31, 12:56 and 2:58 for enlarged recompense. Islāḥī supplies the omitted noun 'outcome': spending and goodness bring good results. Bint al-Shāṭiʾ says this wide sense encompasses monotheism, Paradise and both worldly and otherworldly recompense."}, {"id": "92:6/q03/p11", "position": "Every good quality or real moral good.", "reasons": "Al-Qaffāl cites 9:52, 42:23 and 41:50 for good outcomes and increased reward. Elmalılı says the believer distinguishes virtue from vice. Asad calls ultimate good an absolute moral imperative independent of time and society."}, {"id": "92:6/q03/p12", "position": "The goodness and beneficial purposes of God's prescribed bodily and financial worship.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī join

{"id": "92:6/q04", "question": "Why are giving and piety mentioned before affirmation?", "turns_on": "How the order relates to belief's logical priority, the practical acts, the verse ending and the paired opposite clause.", "positions": [{"id": "92:6/q04/p1", "position": "Affirmation follows piety as a specific instance of a general virtue; its position also preserves the verse ending.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī acknowledges faith's importance while explaining its later placement by the general-to-specific order and rhyme."}, {"id": "92:6/q04/p2", "position": "Giving and piety come first because practical deeds establish the affirmation and lead to its promised result.", "reasons": "Elmalılı says belief precedes deeds in the order of being; the text puts deeds first because verbal belief without them does not earn ease and because effects and recompense follow their causes."}, {"id": "92:6/q04/p3", "position": "Giving heads the paired clauses because it is foundational for the faith and piety or denial and self-sufficiency that follow.", "reasons": "Al-Irshād notes that giving ranks lower than the later traits yet founds their paired descriptions."}, {"id": "92:6/q04/p4", "position": "Giving obedience and avoiding idolatry could be understood as acts that precede faith.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī rejects this explanation: 'giving' conventionally concerns money, especially when opposed to withholding, and the proposed sequence remains unexplained. He also rejects counting listening to learn monotheism as giving and avoidance of shirk as piety."}]}
{"id": "92:6/q05", "question": "What does this affirmation teach about conduct and its result?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "92:6/q05/p1", "position": "Faith in God's good reward motivates giving, piety and perseverance toward the Hereafter.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī says the paired paths lead to praiseworthy or blameworthy outcomes. Elmalılı says expectation of a better afterlife makes sacrifice joyful, citing 59:9 and 64:16. Islāḥī says faith in reward moves one to give for God rather than worldly gain, citing 107:1–3; the struggle against desire grows strength and leads to the company and Paradise of 89:29–30."}, {"id": "92:6/q05/p2", "position": "The three traits express the person's effort toward purification, met by God's freely willed aid.", "reasons": "Sayyid Quṭb says success depends on God's aid despite the person's utmost effort."}, {"id": "92:6/q05/p3", "position": "Giving covers financial worship, piety covers obedience and avoidance of sin, and affirmation covers comprehensive faith.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī prefers the triad because together it covers all endeavors; al-Biqāʿī specifies giving what God commands and guarding oneself through obedience and avoidance."}]}
{"id": "92:6/q06", "question": "How is this verse read inwardly?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "92:6/q06/p1", "position": "Abū Bakr's giving included self and wealth, refusal to settle into the natural self, and affirmation of monotheism.", "reasons": "Tustarī reports this from Abū Bakr."}, {"id": "92:6/q06/p2", "position": "The generous renounce attachment to both abodes, avoid frivolity and doubt, and seek nearness to God.", "reasons": ""}, {"id": "92:6/q06/p3", "position": "Certain faith in the rank of perfection makes ascent possible, and God eases the seeker by cutting attachments and strengthening certainty.", "reasons": "Qāshānī joins intellectual certainty to God's assistance on the easy path."}]}
{"id": "92:6/q07", "question": "Who or what occasion is reported for this passage?", "turns_on": "Different reported persons, transactions and prayers are connected to the revelation.", "positions": [{"id": "92:6/q07/p1", "position": "Abū Bakr freed vulnerable converts despite his father's advice to free strong protectors, seeking God's reward or face.", "reasons": "Al-Farrāʾ gives nine enslaved men bought from polytheists; other reports emphasize weak women or elderly converts. Abū Quḥāfa wanted strong allies, but Abū Bakr sought divine reward or God's face. Al-Ālūsī says al-Ḥākim authenticated the version he cites. Ibn Isḥāq and family reports vary in the father's wording; one report extends the revelation to 'he will be satisfied'."}, {"id": "92:6/q07/p2", "position": "Abū Bakr bought and freed Bilāl from Umayya, and their opposed efforts are contrasted.", "reasons": "Al-Baghawī's anonymous report says the price was a garment and ten coins; Ibn Masʿūd's account also names Ubayy among the opponents. The good is identified as monotheism and the hard outcome as Hell; the contrast relates to 92:4."}, {"id": "92:6/q07/p3", "position": "Abū Bakr is the giver and Abū Sufyān the denier in a report about spending and resurrection.", "reasons": "In Muqātil's report Abū Bakr hopes for forgiveness and promises to remind Abū Sufyān at Saqar; Abū Sufyān mocks resurrection and says spent wealth is lost. The giver is Abū al-Daḥdāḥ and the miser the Anṣārī owner; their ease and hardship lead to Paradise and Hell, while death removes the miser's wealth. Al-Ālūsī notes a similar occasion."}, {"id": "92:6/q07/p5", "position": "An unnamed believer traded forty palms for a stingy owner's tree and gave it to a poor family.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās's report gives forty palms as the price and a promised palm in Paradise for the buyer."}, {"id": "92:6/q07/p6", "position": "The passage was revealed in connection with the angels' prayer for the spender and against the miser.", "reasons": "Reports differ on sunset versus sunrise; the shared prayer requests compensation for the spender and ruin for the withholder. Al-Māwardī states no grading."}]}
{"id": "92:6/q08", "question": "What does the angel report say about spenders and misers?", "turns_on": "The reports differ on sunset versus sunrise or morning.", "positions": [{"id": "92:6/q08/p1", "position": "At sunset two angels pray for the spender's replacement and the miser's loss.", "reasons": "Abū al-Dardāʾ transmits this from the Prophet. {"id": "92:7/q02", "question": "Why does God speak in the first-person plural?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "92:7/q02/p1", "position": "It marks God's authoritative promise and the divine power needed to ease obedience.", "reasons": "Biqāʿī says obedience, though intrinsically easy, burdens the self; Corpus Coranicum says the plural authorizes the paired promises alongside the oath."}]}
{"id": "92:7/q03", "question": "What does nuyassiruhu mean here?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "92:7/q03/p1", "position": "God prepares and makes a person ready for a course or outcome.", "reasons": "Kashshāf, Bayḍāwī, Ālūsī and Elmalılı compare saddling and bridling a horse for riding; Ibn ʿĀshūr says taysīr literally makes something easy to obtain, citing 20:26 and 54:17, and treats 'prepare' as figurative in one analysis."}]}
{"id": "92:7/q04", "question": "How does the object and li- phrase work with nuyassiruhu?", "turns_on": "Whether the ordinary object-beneficiary relation is inverted, li- expresses purpose with figurative preparation, or the words name states while the verb remains literal.", "positions": [{"id": "92:7/q04/p1", "position": "The literal syntax is rhetorically inverted: God eases the easy path for the person.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr observes that normally the direct object is what becomes easy and li- marks its beneficiary, as 20:26 and 54:17 show; inversion intensifies the facilitation. {"id": "92:7/q05", "question": "Whom does the pronoun refer to?", "turns_on": "Whether the preceding description is taken generally or identified with the reported occasions involving Abū Bakr or the palm purchase.", "positions": [{"id": "92:7/q05/p1", "position": "The giver who fears God and affirms His promise, described in the preceding verses; the pattern applies generally.", "reasons": "Ṭabarī identifies the generous God-fearing believer; Ibn ʿĀshūr says the clauses mark faith, with omitted object of 'fears' understood as God and compares 74:43–44. {"id": "92:7/q06", "question": "What does God make easy for this person in practice?", "turns_on": "Whether the promised ease is chiefly enabled conduct, renewed conduct, a pleasant state in both lives, or entry to Paradise; Ṭabāṭabāʾ explicitly favors the afterlife emphasis.", "positions": [{"id": "92:7/q06/p1", "position": "God enables pleasing and righteous deeds until obedience becomes easy.", "reasons": "Ṭabarī locates these deeds in this life and Paradise as their reward; Māwardī and Qurṭubī stress making the means easy; Qushayrī adds love of faith and excellence, hatred of disobedience, and desire for nearness. Kashshāf compares opening the breast to Islam (6:125); Rāzī contrasts hypocritical sluggishness (2:45, 4:142, 9:38). Ṭabrisī stresses repeated, eager obedience; Islahi adds removal of obstacles and strengthened desire (29:69); Kur'an Yolu says generosity becomes a stable trait; Quṭb describes calm ease spreading through worldly life."}, {"id": "92:7/q06/p2", "position": "God eases a return to earlier obedience, especially renewed giving.", "reasons": "Farrāʾ and Ibn Qutayba describe a return to righteous acts; Muqātil specifies repeated giving, while Qushayrī mentions resuming worship. {"id": "92:7/q07", "question": "What is al-yusrā?", "turns_on": "Whether yusrā names deeds or their course, Paradise and its reward, or a broader easy state spanning both lives.", "positions": [{"id": "92:7/q07/p1", "position": "The easy course of goodness, obedience and deeds pleasing to God.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās repeatedly glosses it as good; Ṭabarī, Thaʿlabī, Baghawī and Nasafī call it approved deeds. Ibn ʿĀshūr says it broadly means what benefits without hardship."}, {"id": "92:7/q07/p2", "position": "Paradise, the good destination or ease of afterlife bliss.", "reasons": "Zayd ibn Aslam and Mujāhid are named repeatedly; Ṭabrisī includes angelic welcome; Rāzī says the promised Paradise makes strenuous worship bearable. {"id": "92:7/q12", "question": "What does facilitation teach about deeds and divine decree?", "turns_on": "How divine preparation and prior knowledge relate to human acts; the reports repeatedly answer the temptation to rely on decree by commanding work.", "positions": [{"id": "92:7/q12/p1", "position": "Destinations are written or known beforehand, yet people must act; each is enabled for the deeds associated with that end.", "reasons": "ʿAlī's funeral report appears across sources and is graded ḥasan ṣaḥīḥ by Tirmidhī in Qurṭubī; Ibn ʿĀshūr names Bukhārī. {"id": "92:7/q15", "question": "How does this promise fit the sūra's paired paths?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "92:7/q15/p1", "position": "It is the good half of the paired sequence: conduct leads to felicity, while opposed conduct leads to hardship.", "reasons": "Ṭabarī contrasts the giver with the self-sufficient miser; Rāzī explains divergent striving and reward or punishment.
